newsitem.title: USA: IMF board may recommend expulsion of Sudan.
newsitem.headline: IMF board may recommend expulsion of Sudan.

text.p: The executive board of the International Monetary Fund, in an almost unprecedented action, may recommend that Sudan be expelled from the lending agency because of a refusal to deal with its huge debt, monetary sources said on Thursday.

The 24-member executive board meets on Jan. 31 to review Sudan's financial situation and may recommend that IMF-member countries vote to remove the African state from the agency when they gather at the annual meeting this fall.

However, the sources made clear that even if the voting members of the executive board agree by 50 percent to expel Sudan as required, it is far less likely that the member countries will follow suit in sufficient strength to achieve the required 85 percent majority needed to expel.
It is thought that even those developing countries that have little sympathy for Sudan would be reluctant to act against one of their own, according to the sources.
"There is a real question if at the end of the day Sudan will actually be kicked out," said one source.
Ironically, the possibility of a country being forced out of the IMF comes at a time when its membership is greatest.

Membership in the institution, formed in the last days of the Second World War, has risen substantially in recent years to 181 countries as the independent states of the former Soviet Union and others have signed on.

While some countries have chosen to leave the lending institution voluntarily, IMF records show only one country -- Czechoslovakia -- was compelled to withdraw because it refused to provide required economic data in the early 1950s.
The IMF estimates Sudan is $1.7 billion in arrears on its loans, and Khartoum has shown little interest in rescheduling or other measures to solve the problem, the sources said.
Jose Pedro de Morais, an IMF alternate executive director, said in Khartoum on Wednesday that Sudan's case was also being hurt by perceptions the country was an Islamic fundamentalist state.
"Unless there are impressive changes on how the Sudanese government is perceived outside, I don't see any possibility to avoid a compulsory withdrawal decision," he told Reuters.
He said Washington in particular had argued in the past that Sudan should be expelled if it did not make some arrangement to repay its arrears.
The United States has also taken the view that Sudan is one of seven countries supporting terrorism and has cut off some trade, including arms sales.
One of the poorest countries in the world, Sudan is also facing a rebel offensive.
As it now stands, Sudan is one of four countries ineligible to borrow from the IMF because of overdue loans and has also lost its voting rights in the institution.
